slides.headline: 500 years later, nobody knows what this is
A painting without answers
slides.text: Venice, early 1500s. Giorgione paints a soldier, a nursing mother and a storm for a nobleman. Nobody ever wrote down what it means.

slides.headline: The storm
slides.text: Above the town, lightning cracks the sky. Around 1530, a visitor described it simply: a small landscape with the storm, a gypsy and a soldier.

slides.headline: The soldier
slides.text: On the left, a young man in fine clothes leans on a staff. He looks across the stream toward her. Soldier? Shepherd? Nobody knows.

slides.headline: She's watching you
slides.text: On the right, a nearly naked woman nurses a baby. She ignores him and looks straight at us, as if we interrupted something.

slides.headline: Broken columns
slides.text: Between them, two broken columns stand on a ruined wall, leading nowhere. A clue, or just decoration? And then came the X-rays.

slides.headline: The woman underneath
slides.text: In 1939 they revealed a surprise: the soldier wasn't there at first. Giorgione had painted another nude woman, seated in his place.

slides.headline: Over 100 theories
slides.text: So what is it? Adam and Eve with baby Cain? Paris and his nurse? Fortitude and Charity? Scholars have proposed over a hundred theories.

slides.headline: Your turn
slides.text: Maybe Giorgione wanted no single story at all. Lord Byron reportedly loved it for exactly that. So what do you think is happening here?
